The Architecture of FearExploring Spaces in Resident Evil, Obsession, and The Backrooms

This project asks a simple question: why do some buildings feel frightening before anything happens in them? I look at three horror films from 2002, 2025 and 2026, and at how each one uses rooms, corridors and doorways to unsettle its audience.

01Overview

The three films come from different years and have different stories, but all three get their tension from the layout of a place. Each one is afraid of a different kind of space.

Resident Evil is afraid of a house with something hidden under it. Obsession is afraid of an ordinary bedroom where a wish goes wrong. Backrooms is afraid of a door in a store basement that opens onto endless rooms.
Resident Evil

A house on top of a hidden lab

A quiet mansion that hides the way down to an underground research facility.

Obsession

Small rooms and a wish gone wrong

Everyday bedrooms and shared spaces where a wish turns a relationship into a trap.

The Backrooms

A doorway to endless rooms

A door in a store basement opens onto identical, fluorescent-lit spaces with no clear way out.

06Bibliography

Works cited, MLA style.

  2. Augé, Marc. Non-Places: Introduction to an Anthropology of Supermodernity. Translated by John Howe, Verso, 1995.
  3. Bachelard, Gaston. The Poetics of Space. Translated by Maria Jolas, Beacon Press, 1994.
  4. Barker, Curry, director. Obsession. Focus Features, 2025.
  5. Fisher, Mark. The Weird and the Eerie. Repeater Books, 2016.
  6. Foucault, Michel. Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison. Translated by Alan Sheridan, Vintage, 1995.
  7. Freud, Sigmund. “The Uncanny.” The Standard Edition of the Complete Psychological Works of Sigmund Freud, vol. 17, Hogarth Press, 1955, pp. 217–56.
  8. Parsons, Kane, director. Backrooms. A24, 2026.
  9. Parsons, Kane. “The Backrooms (Found Footage).” YouTube, 2022.
  10. Tuan, Yi-Fu. Space and Place: The Perspective of Experience. U of Minnesota P, 1977.
  11. Vidler, Anthony. The Architectural Uncanny: Essays in the Modern Unhomely. MIT Press, 1992.
